metadata.title: Why a Perfect Explanation Can Make You More Wrong
metadata.topic: EXPLAINABILITY & INTERPRETABILITY · SHORTCUT LEARNING & FLUENCY TRAP
metadata.purpose: Answer one real question in the Plain register: why can an accurate AI explanation make you more confident in a wrong decision? Lands the carry-out that explanations faithfully describe a model's internal accounting, including learned shortcuts, transferring unearned confidence to the human.
metadata.anchor_pair: B06 -> B07/B08 (Two-Path Decision: Prediction Alone vs Prediction + Explanation)
metadata.one_flag: B10 — transparency of internal math is not proof of truth in deployment

beats.narration_text: When an AI tool gives an accurate explanation, you assume it makes human decisions more reliable. In practice, a truthful explanation can make you far more confident in a wrong call. Let's see why.

shot.new_visual_element: Writer types naive question, hesitates on 'strictly more reliable', corrects to 'sometimes dangerously wrong'

props.text:
If an AI's explanation is accurate,
doesn't it make our decisions
strictly more reliable?

beats.note: B00 is Remotion (BrutalistHesitantWriter) per course-skepticism SKILL.md. Writer types naive framing, hesitates, corrects to sometimes dangerously wrong. Liam reads final corrected question over typing animation.

beats.narration_text: A radiologist reviews a screening image. An AI tool predicts high risk of malignancy at eighty-four percent confidence. And the system provides an explanation: the prediction was driven by texture pattern X and asymmetry Y.

shot.new_visual_element: Screening interface card with AI risk prediction 84%, feature highlights X and Y, and composite case label

production_viz.label: The Explainable AI Screening Tool
production_viz.mechanic: Interface card showing Screening Risk Score 84% (Malignancy), driven by Feature X (Texture) and Feature Y (Asymmetry). Stamped COMPOSITE CLINICAL ILLUSTRATION.

beats.narration_text: The radiologist looks at the image. Feature X is there. Feature Y is there. The explanation feels coherent, so she concurs and orders a biopsy. The biopsy comes back completely benign.

shot.new_visual_element: Radiologist inspection card confirming features X and Y, biopsy recommendation, and stamp: BENIGN OUTCOME

production_viz.label: False Concurrence & Benign Truth
production_viz.mechanic: Two verification boxes for Features X & Y checked green, leading to invasive biopsy recommendation, stamped with Benign Outcome in ink/terracotta.

beats.narration_text: The natural reaction is to assume the AI hallucinated or gave a fake explanation. But the explanation was completely accurate: the model really used features X and Y. The model did not lie about itself.

shot.new_visual_element: Wrong guess card: Assumption that explanation was fake/hallucinated struck through with terracotta line

production_viz.label: The Explanation Fallacy
production_viz.mechanic: Card reading 'Assumption: The explanation was hallucinated' struck through with a terracotta bar. True status: Model computation was 100% faithful to internal weights.

beats.narration_text: What happened is shortcut learning. In training, features X and Y correlated with cancer cases. But in this patient's population, those same features belong to a benign condition. The model learned a shortcut.

shot.new_visual_element: Shortcut learning diagram: Training data correlation vs deployment reality

production_viz.label: Shortcut Learning
production_viz.mechanic: Split visual: Training Set (Features X & Y correlate with Malignancy) vs Deployment Set (Features X & Y appear in Benign condition). Status: Learned Shortcut.

beats.narration_text: Post-hoc explanations faithfully describe a model's internal accounting. They tell you what the model did. They cannot tell you whether what the model did warrants belief about the real world.

shot.new_visual_element: Two columns: Internal Accounting (What Model Did) vs State of the World (What Is True)

production_viz.label: Internal Accounting vs The World
production_viz.mechanic: Two side-by-side columns: Column 1 (Model's Internal Accounting: Faithful description of weights) vs Column 2 (State of the World: Independent biological ground truth).

beats.narration_text: To see how this misleads, compare two ways a clinician evaluates an AI output: seeing the prediction alone, versus seeing the prediction paired with an explanation.

shot.new_visual_element: Two-Path Decision Flow diagram: Path A (Prediction Alone) vs Path B (Prediction + Explanation)

production_viz.label: The Two-Path Decision Flow
production_viz.mechanic: Flowchart branching into Path A: Prediction Alone [Score Only] and Path B: Prediction + Explanation [Score + Feature Highlights].

beats.narration_text: In Path A, the doctor sees only the eighty-four percent score. Because she knows classifiers can be noisy, she treats the score with healthy skepticism, keeping her confidence balanced at fifty percent.

shot.new_visual_element: MANIM MOVE compare (Panel A): Prediction Alone with confidence meter balanced at 50% (Cautious Review)

production_viz.label: Path A: Prediction Alone
production_viz.mechanic: Left panel: Score 84% received with no story. Human Confidence Meter stays at 50% (Cautious Skepticism). Label: Healthy Doubt.

beats.narration_text: In Path B, she sees the exact same score alongside the highlighted features. Because the story is plausible and verifiable, her confidence surges to ninety percent — locking in an aggressive, mistaken decision.

shot.new_visual_element: MANIM MOVE compare (Panel B): Prediction + Explanation with confidence meter surging to 90% (Overconfident Error)

production_viz.label: Path B: Prediction + Explanation
production_viz.mechanic: Right panel: Score 84% + Features X & Y story. Human Confidence Meter surges from 50% to 90% in terracotta. Label: Unearned Confidence.

beats.narration_text: This is the fluency trap: well-formed outputs are mistaken for evidence of truth. The explanation gave a flawed decision a convincing narrative, transferring unearned confidence from the machine's accounting to the human mind.

shot.new_visual_element: The Fluency Trap: Well-formed story -> unearned epistemic confidence transfer

production_viz.label: The Fluency Trap
production_viz.mechanic: Diagram showing Coherent Story -> Unearned Epistemic Weight -> Human Overconfidence. The trap is fluency masquerading as validation.

beats.narration_text: One flag — an explanation provides transparency into a model's internal computation, but transparency of math is not proof of truth in deployment. Inspecting internal weights does not validate reality.

shot.new_visual_element: The One Flag: Transparency of internal computation is not validation of external reality

production_viz.label: The One Flag: Transparency vs Truth
production_viz.mechanic: Flag badge: Transparency (Inspectable internal weights) ≠ Truth (Valid external mapping). Inspecting computation does not validate the world.

beats.narration_text: So in one direction, a perfectly faithful explanation does not prove the model is right. It may simply give you a pristine, high-fidelity view of a broken shortcut.

shot.new_visual_element: Direction A: Faithful explanation does not equal correct decision

production_viz.label: Direction A: Accurate Explanation ≠ Correct Model
production_viz.mechanic: Card: 100% Faithful Explanation does not imply Correct Decision. It is a high-fidelity view of internal accounting.

beats.narration_text: And in the other direction, a wrong decision does not mean the explanation tool lied. It did its job by exposing the model's logic — leaving the skepticism to us.

shot.new_visual_element: Direction B: Flawed decision does not mean dishonest explanation; human supervision supplies the doubt

production_viz.label: Direction B: Flawed Model ≠ Dishonest Explanation
production_viz.mechanic: Card: Flawed Prediction does not imply Dishonest Tool. The explanation tool exposed the model; human supervision supplies the skepticism.

beats.narration_text: A faithful explanation describes the model's internal accounting, not the world — so when a model learns a shortcut, an accurate explanation makes a wrong call feel right.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here's the prompt — read it with me. Take a deployed classifier in your stack that provides feature explanations. Audit five cases where the model made an error. Did the explanation faithfully describe the model's shortcut, and would reading it make a reviewer more likely to approve the mistake? Liam, in for Bear.
